reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A malignant embryonal tumour of the pineal region, most often affecting children, and the highest-grade pineal parenchymal tumour
Midline location commonly compresses the tectal plate and aqueduct, causing obstructive hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation)
Occurs in the germline RB1 predisposition setting as trilateral retinoblastoma, where bilateral retinoblastoma coexists with a pineal or suprasellar embryonal tumour
Germline DICER1 mutations are also associated and define a distinct molecular subset
Frequently disseminates through the cerebrospinal fluid, so full neuraxis staging is required
Distinguished from more indolent pineal parenchymal tumours of intermediate differentiation and from pineocytoma by its high cellularity and mitotic activity
Management combines maximal safe resection, craniospinal radiotherapy where age permits, and chemotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Pineoblastoma is a poorly differentiated embryonal tumour arising from the parenchymal cells of the pineal gland. It shows primitive small round cells with high proliferative activity and a propensity to seed the cerebrospinal fluid pathways. A proportion of cases arise on a background of germline predisposition, most notably biallelic RB1 loss (the basis of trilateral retinoblastoma, in which a pineal or suprasellar tumour accompanies bilateral hereditary retinoblastoma) and germline DICER1 mutations, which impair microRNA processing. Its midline position adjacent to the tectum and cerebral aqueduct means that even modest growth readily obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow and compresses the dorsal midbrain.
additionalDifferentials: Pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation
Papillary tumour of the pineal region
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the pineal mass and hydrocephalus
Craniospinal MRI to assess for leptomeningeal dissemination
CSF cytology and serum/CSF germ cell tumour markers to exclude germinoma or non-germinomatous tumours
Ophthalmological examination for retinoblastoma and germline RB1 testing
Germline DICER1 testing where the clinical picture suggests it
redFlags: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with rapidly rising intracranial pressure
Progressive dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) signs and deteriorating consciousness
Evidence of CSF dissemination along the neuraxis
Coexisting bilateral retinoblastoma indicating trilateral disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded and worse than for lower-grade pineal parenchymal tumours, being poorest in infants, those with metastatic disease, and germline RB1-associated trilateral retinoblastoma. Combined surgery, craniospinal radiotherapy and chemotherapy can achieve durable control in older children with localised disease, but survivors are at risk of significant treatment-related late effects.
pitfalls: Mistaking a pineal germ cell tumour for pineoblastoma without checking serum and CSF tumour markers
Failing to examine the eyes and test germline RB1 in a child with a pineal embryonal tumour
Attributing early upgaze failure to a benign cause and missing tectal compression
Understaging by omitting craniospinal imaging and CSF cytology
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
